title: Things to Do in Chittorgarh: Exploring India's Largest Fort
seoTitle: Things to Do in Chittorgarh: Fort, Towers & Palaces | Kudozz Club
description: Things to do in Chittorgarh: explore the fort's Vijay Stambh and Kirti Stambh, Rani Padmini's palace, Meera Temple and Rana Kumbha's palace, watch the evening sound and light show, and see nearby Bassi and Menal.
dek: A fort covering some 700 acres on a mesa above the plains, holding towers of victory, temples, palaces and the stories of Rajasthan's most famous sieges.
searchIntent: History-minded travellers visiting Chittorgarh as a day trip from Udaipur or a stop between Udaipur and Jaipur.

hero.alt: Vijay Stambh, the Tower of Victory, at Chittorgarh Fort
hero.caption: Vijay Stambh

intro: Chittorgarh Fort, capital of Mewar for around 800 years, is one of the largest forts in India, spread over roughly 700 acres on a plateau about 180 metres above the surrounding plains. It was besieged three times, by Alauddin Khalji in 1303, Bahadur Shah of Gujarat in 1535 and Akbar in 1568, and each defeat is remembered in stories of jauhar and saka. It is part of the UNESCO Hill Forts of Rajasthan.

Almost everything worth doing in Chittorgarh is inside the fort. A circuit road links its gates, towers, palaces and temples, and a full day with a car or auto-rickshaw lets you see it properly. The town below is a practical base; Udaipur is about two hours away.

sections.heading: Inside Chittorgarh Fort
sections.intro: Allow at least half a day, ideally a full day, for the fort. Hiring a local guide at the gate makes the stories and ruins much easier to follow.

items.name: Climb the Vijay Stambh
body: The nine-storey Tower of Victory was built by Rana Kumbha in the 15th century to mark a victory over the Sultan of Malwa. Every surface is carved with Hindu deities. A narrow internal stair climbs to the top, with views across the fort. It is the fort's defining landmark and the symbol of Mewar.

facts.Good to know: The stairway is narrow and steep

items.name: See the Kirti Stambh

image.alt: Kirti Stambh, the Tower of Fame, Chittorgarh
image.caption: Kirti Stambh

body: Older and smaller than the Vijay Stambh, the 12th-century Kirti Stambh (Tower of Fame) was built by a Jain merchant and is dedicated to Adinatha, the first Jain tirthankara. It is decorated with Jain figures and stands beside a temple.

items.name: Visit Rani Padmini's Palace
body: Padmini's Palace is a white building beside a lotus pool, with a small pavilion in the water. According to legend, Alauddin Khalji was allowed to see Rani Padmini's reflection here, which led to the siege of 1303. Historians debate the legend, but the palace and its setting are central to Chittorgarh's story.

items.name: See the Meera and Kumbha Shyam temples
body: Meera Bai, the 16th-century poet-saint devoted to Krishna, lived at Chittorgarh as a Mewar princess. The Meera Temple stands in the same compound as the larger Kumbha Shyam Temple, built in the Indo-Aryan style with a tall spire.

items.name: Explore Rana Kumbha's Palace
body: The ruins of Rana Kumbha's 15th-century palace are the oldest monument in the fort. This is where Udai Singh, the founder of Udaipur, is said to have been born, and where the loyal nurse Panna Dai saved him as an infant by sacrificing her own son. The ruins of the zenana and the jauhar site are nearby.

items.name: See Gaumukh Kund
body: Gaumukh Kund is a reservoir fed by a spring that flows from a rock carved as a cow's mouth. It was an important water source during sieges, and its cliffside setting is peaceful.

items.name: See the fort's gates
body: The road up to the fort passes through seven gates (pols), including Padan Pol, Bhairon Pol, Hanuman Pol, Ganesh Pol and Ram Pol. Memorials near some of them honour warriors who fell in the sieges, such as Jaimal and Patta during Akbar's attack. Stopping at a couple of them on the way up sets the scene.

items.name: Visit Fateh Prakash Palace Museum
body: Built in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Maharana Fateh Singh, this palace inside the fort houses a museum of sculpture, weapons and local crafts. It is a useful stop for context before exploring the older ruins.

items.name: Watch the sound and light show
body: An evening sound and light show at the fort narrates the history of the sieges and the rulers of Mewar. Check the language schedule, as shows alternate between Hindi and English on different days.

items.name: Bassi and Menal
body: Bassi Wildlife Sanctuary and the Bassi Fort palace (now a hotel) lie about 25 km east. Further towards Bundi, Menal has a gorge, a seasonal waterfall and a cluster of 11th-century Shiva temples, a good stop if you are driving on to Bundi.

items.name: Sanwariya Seth Temple
body: About 40 km from Chittorgarh on the Udaipur road, the Sanwariya Seth (Krishna) temple is one of the most visited in the region, with an elaborately decorated modern complex. Many travellers stop here in transit.

oneDay: Enter the fort in the morning and follow the circuit road: Rana Kumbha's Palace, the Meera and Kumbha Shyam temples, the Vijay Stambh, Gaumukh Kund, Padmini's Palace and the Kirti Stambh. After a late lunch in town, return for the sound and light show.

faqs.q: What are the best things to do in Chittorgarh?
faqs.a: Explore Chittorgarh Fort: climb the Vijay Stambh, see the Kirti Stambh, Padmini's Palace, the Meera Temple and Rana Kumbha's Palace, and watch the evening sound and light show.

faqs.q: How much time do you need at Chittorgarh Fort?
faqs.a: At least half a day, ideally a full day. The fort covers about 700 acres, and a car or auto-rickshaw is needed to get between sights.

faqs.q: Can Chittorgarh be done as a day trip from Udaipur?
faqs.a: Yes. It is about two hours by road, and many travellers visit on a day trip or stop on the way between Udaipur and Jaipur or Bundi.
Its vast fort, the Vijay Stambh, the legend of Rani Padmini, the poet-saint Meera Bai and the three great sieges of 1303, 1535 and 1568.

byTraveller.text: Hire a local guide at the gate, visit the museum first for context, then follow the circuit through the ruins, gates and towers.
The Vijay Stambh climb, the lotus pool at Padmini's Palace and the evening show make the fort engaging for older children.

tips: The fort is large; hire an auto-rickshaw or bring a car for the circuit road rather than trying to walk it all.
There is little shade on the plateau, so carry water and a hat, especially outside winter.
The Vijay Stambh's interior stair is dark and narrow; skip it if you are claustrophobic.
Chittorgarh has a railway junction with connections to Udaipur, Jaipur and Delhi, and sits on the main highway between Udaipur and Jaipur.
